lines.text: Classic cocktails are the foundation of mixology — recipes that have endured for decades or centuries because their balance of flavours is timeless. The Old Fashioned, arguably the original cocktail, combines whisky (bourbon or rye), sugar, bitters, and a twist of orange peel — spirit-forward, aromatic, and elegant. The Martini — gin or vodka stirred with dry vermouth — epitomises sophistication; 'dry' means less vermouth, 'dirty' adds olive brine. The Negroni, an Italian classic adopted by British cocktail culture, balances gin, sweet vermouth, and Campari in equal parts — bitter, complex, and deceptively strong. The Daiquiri — rum, fresh lime juice, and sugar — is the bartender's benchmark: if a bar makes a good Daiquiri, everything else will be reliable. The Margarita pairs tequila with lime and orange liqueur, served in a salt-rimmed glass. The Whisky Sour combines whisky with lemon juice, sugar, and optionally egg white for a silky foam. The Mojito — rum, fresh mint, lime, sugar, and soda — is the quintessential summer refresher. The Espresso Martini, invented in London in the 1980s by bartender Dick Bradsell, has become Britain's most ordered cocktail — vodka, espresso, coffee liqueur, and sugar syrup, shaken until frothy. Each classic follows a template: a base spirit, a modifier (sweet, sour, or bitter), and a seasoning (bitters, salt, or aromatics).

lines.text: 'Cocktail hour' — typically 5pm to 7pm — is when many British bars offer discounted drinks and when after-work socialising peaks. 'Shall we go for cocktails after work?' is a standard Friday invitation. The concept bridges the gap between the working day and evening plans.

lines.text: Many classic cocktails were created or refined during American Prohibition (1920–1933), when bartenders fled to London, Paris, and Havana. The Savoy Hotel's American Bar in London became a cocktail destination. Harry Craddock's 'Savoy Cocktail Book' (1930) remains a definitive reference.

lines.text: Modern British cocktail bars prioritise inclusivity — extensive non-alcoholic menus, allergen awareness (nut liqueurs, egg white alternatives), and drinks suitable for all dietary requirements. 'Can you make that vegan?' is a standard question — aquafaba (chickpea water) replaces egg white in sours.
